17: . O . X .

19:   O O O X .
20:    . X O X O
21:     X O O O X
22: ```
23: 
24: "Player `O`" plays from top to bottom, "Player `X`" plays from left to right.
25: In the above example `O` has made a connection from left to right but nobody has won since `O` didn't connect top and bottom.

part.text:
Now I understand the problem. This is the classic Hex/CON-TAC-TIX game. Key points:

- The board is a parallelogram drawn with each row indented by one additional space (half a hex cell). After the test strips the spaces, each row becomes a simple string.
- For a cell `(r, c)`, its 6 neighbors in this layout are `(r-1, c)`, `(r-1, c+1)`, `(r, c-1)`, `(r, c+1)`, `(r+1, c-1)`, `(r+1, c)` (each row shifts half a cell to the right).
- `O` connects the top row to the bottom row, and `X` connects the left edge to the right edge.

I'll implement this with a BFS from all of a player's stones on their starting side:

part.text:
All tests pass. Here's a summary of the implementation in `connect.go`:

## Solution

**`ResultOf(lines []string) (string, error)`** — builds a grid from the lines (the leading spaces are just visual indentation, so after the test's `prepare` strips them, each line is a plain row of cells), then checks `O` and `X` in turn.

**`connects(grid, player)`** — a flood fill (iterative DFS with a visited matrix) seeded from all of the player's stones on their *start* side:
- `O`: start = top row, finish = bottom row (connects top to bottom)
- `X`: start = left edge (col 0), finish = right edge (last col of the row)

The key geometric detail is the neighbor set. Since each row of the parallelogram is shifted half a cell to the right, the six neighbors of cell `(r, c)` are:

```
(r-1, c)  (r-1, c+1)
(r, c-1)  (r, c+1)
(r+1, c-1)(r+1, c)
```

(Not the naive `(r+1, c)` / `(r+1, c+1)` — that convention fails the "O wins crossing from top to bottom" case, where the top `O` only connects downward-left.)

Boundary checks use each row's own length, so boards with mismatched width/height (like the 5×4 test boards) work correctly. The 1×1 cases win because the single cell is simultaneously on the start and finish side.

Verification: `go test -v ./...` — all 10 cases pass, and `go vet` is clean. No other files were modified.
